--- ABSTRACT ---
This study aimed to review the current literature for epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical spectrum and management of rhino-orbito-cerebral-mucormycosis (ROCM), especially highlighting the association between ROCM and COVID-19 disease and factors resulting in its resurgence during the pandemic. Mucormycosis is a rare, but an important emerging opportunistic fungal infection, often associated with high morbidity and mortality. ROCM is the commonest and also the most aggressive clinical form occurring in debilitated patients in conjunction with sinus or para-sinus involvement due to the propensity for contiguous spread. Recently ROCM has shown an unprecedented resurgence during the current pandemic. Reports from different parts of the world indicated an increased risk and incidence of ROCM in patients who had required hospital admission and have recovered from moderate-to-severe COVID-19 disease. A majority of mucormycosis cases have been reported from India. The presence of diabetes mellitus (DM) and use of corticosteroids for COVID-19 pneumonia were found to be the key risk factors, resulting in higher mortality. Amidst the ongoing pandemic, with the third wave already having affected most of the world, it becomes imperative to adopt a risk-based approach toward COVID-19 patients predisposed to developing ROCM. This could be based on the most recently published literature and emerging data from centers across the world. The present review intended to elucidate the causes that brought about the current spike in ROCM and the importance of its early detection and management to reduce mortality, loss of eye, and the need for mutilating debridement.

key_findings.finding: The presentation is most consistent with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis (ROCM), an acute invasive Mucorales sinus infection favored by poorly controlled diabetes and immunosuppression (including HIV); maxillary sinus disease with black necrotic eschar of the nares/palate is a classic angioinvasive pattern. Definitive diagnosis requires urgent endoscopic evaluation and tissue demonstrating fungal hyphae by histopathology/culture, but this is a clinical emergency and treatment should not await confirmation.

source_tools.relevance: ROCM review identifies it as an aggressive opportunistic infection in debilitated patients and highlights diabetes as a major risk factor.
PubMed search retrieved literature describing rhino-sino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis and diagnostic confirmation by KOH, culture, or histopathology.
Search results identify mucormycosis as the relevant disease in diabetic patients with rhino-orbital involvement.

key_findings.finding: Among the listed symptoms, impaired extraocular movements (ophthalmoplegia/EOM restriction) is the strongest single indicator of extension to the orbital apex or cavernous sinus; it reflects involvement of the extraocular motor nerves/muscles and is supported by an ROCM observational study reporting extraocular movement restriction and cavernous-sinus involvement as common neurologic/orbital manifestations. Ptosis, diplopia, proptosis with chemosis, decreased corneal reflex, and V2 numbness are important accompanying cranial-nerve/orbital signs but are generally less specific individually.

source_tools.relevance: The ROCM observational study explicitly reports proptosis, vision loss, and extraocular movement restriction, with cavernous sinus involvement, and describes involvement of the optic nerve and extraocular muscles.
Imaging review states that spread to the cavernous sinus can occur via the orbital apex.

key_findings.finding: If the question is specifically asking for the strongest sign of intracranial rather than orbital-apical/cavernous-sinus extension, altered mental status is the most concerning choice; it suggests cerebral/meningeal involvement. Thus, clinically: choose impaired extraocular movements for orbital apex/cavernous sinus disease, while altered mental status signals possible intracranial spread and warrants immediate neuroimaging and specialist escalation.

source_tools.relevance: The ROCM study documents meningeal and parenchymal involvement as part of neuroaxis disease.
The imaging-spectrum paper describes spread from the orbital apex to the cavernous sinus and toward the frontal lobe via ophthalmic arteries/cribriform plate.
